JAGS is not the only program that turns a model description into an MCMC sampler.
Stan [@carpenter2017stan] is the other one most courses use,
and the two answer the same question in different ways.
Both take a model written in their own language,
accept data from R,
and return draws from the [posterior](bayesian-inference.qmd#def-posterior).
They differ in how they draw and in what a model may contain.

JAGS builds a [Gibbs sampler](mcmc.qmd#def-gibbs-sampler) from the model's description
[@plummer2003jags; @plummer2017jagsmanual].
It chooses a sampling method for each [full conditional](mcmc.qmd#def-full-conditional),
using slice or Metropolis--Hastings steps where the full conditional has no closed form.
Stan uses Hamiltonian Monte Carlo,
which proposes moves along the gradient of the logarithm of the [posterior](bayesian-inference.qmd#def-posterior),
in the adaptive form called the No-U-Turn sampler (NUTS)
[@hoffman2014nuts].
Using the gradient is why Stan cannot draw a [discrete](data.qmd#def-discrete-var) parameter:
a discrete parameter has no gradient.
A Stan model sums a discrete quantity out of the [likelihood](intro-MLEs.qmd#def-lik) instead
[@stanusersguide].
The table lists the practical differences:

```{r}
#| label: tbl-stan-vs-jags
#| tbl-cap: "JAGS and Stan compared"
#| echo: false
knitr::kable(
  read.csv("data/bayes-software.csv"),
  col.names = c("Feature", "JAGS", "Stan"),
  format = "pipe"
)
```

The table's rows are in [`data/bayes-software.csv`](data/bayes-software.csv).
The next example fits the model of [the first example](#exm-bayes-proportion) in Stan,
so the two programs can be compared on one problem.
